candidates.text:
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes.

With everything happening around AI, it feels like we’ve seen versions of this story before. Technologies change, industries get disrupted, and businesses that once seemed permanent disappear.

The latest episode of Intermission by @TheKenWeb is on TCS, and one thing stood out to me. In the 1960s, India had only a few dozen computers, and even that was enough for unions to protest, fearing they would take away jobs. TCS was started around the same time, and over the next few decades, it and the rest of the IT industry went on to employ millions of Indians. Now the same industry is dealing with a new version of that fear, with AI starting to do some of the work that people used to do.

I didn’t know this story, and I think most people don’t either. It’s the kind of detail that gets lost with time. Businesses, like people, come and go. Which is all the more reason to document them well. How they were built, the decisions that worked and didn’t, the mistakes, the people, the culture, and all the little stories that would otherwise disappear.

We spend a lot of time documenting history through countries, wars, politics, and famous people. Maybe we need to do a much better job of documenting the history of businesses too. There’s probably a lot for future entrepreneurs to learn from them🙂

candidates.text:
I pointed Claude at the below post and it embedded all 146,060 Steam games, sampled 320,000 points between them, ranked them by how far they land from anything that exists, and used creative judgment to pick a winner... and it cooked!

It's pick: Short Position, a co-op factory tycoon where one player has secretly shorted the stock.

4–8 players run one industrial empire: mines, smelters, rail, contracts. There’s no kill button and no sabotage minigame. The traitor plays the factory game badly on purpose. Overbuild a warehouse, route ore to the wrong smelter, sign a contract with a penalty clause on page 4. Every move looks like an honest mistake.

The twist is that suspicion is expensive. Anyone can audit the production logs, but audits cost money and spook investors. The traitor doesn’t need to wreck the factory. They just need everyone paranoid enough to do it themselves.

Each quarter ends with an earnings call and a board vote. Fire an honest exec and you lose their whole department. Four quarters, ~40 minutes.

It sits farther from its nearest neighbors than 83% of real Steam games. Factory games have co-op, social deduction games have tasks, and nobody has made the work itself the place where you lie.

candidates.text:
Intelligence without wisdom is often how you end up getting what you want, only to notice, way too late, that it wasn't what you wanted, but what everybody else wanted in a mimetically contagious process.

The price of figuring out what you truly want from life is time alone, and most people never really grow enough courage to isolate themselves long enough, and never discover their core values as a result.

Lack of simple joy and genuine smiles in your daily life, lingering anxiety and anger for no specific reason, emotional distance even with your family and friends, or no close family or friend at all, and a feeling of emptiness despite becoming more and more conventionally "successful" to the eyes of society; these are all signs that you are not walking the journey you should be walking.

candidates.text:
One of the worst things that naive young people can do is to believe that they're gonna be handed over a future of abundance where money won't matter, where everybody's needs will be fulfilled, where they will no longer have to compete to get what they want.

Not only the gap between people who own assets and people who don't has clearly only widened throughout the last few decades,

but the gap of mental health and self-esteem has also only gotten increasingly bigger between clear thinkers and driven people, and the others (despite a wider access to knowledge and opportunities),

and that's because once you give up on chasing a better and more competitive version of yourself, you become directionless and motionless, and the default state when you don't move meaningfully is anxiety accumulation:

you realize that the difficult challenges that forced you to grow also brought, in retrospect, a lot of peace and joy into your daily life, and that they were actually not something that you wanted to be relieved from.

candidates.text:
historically, being an inference provider was kinda buns

low-ish margins and not enough demand

but now demand has skyrocketed, and with spec dec and model assisted custom kernel development you can make absurd margins, especially on dedicated compute

which would be great already, but this compute you’re using is a actually appreciating!!

this is why morph/relace/wafer/baseten/inference net are all crushing rn

serving kimi-sized models is still lots of work (you also can’t vibe code four nines) so they can serve any specific workload 70%+ cheaper plus and charge margin on top of that, and customers are happy bc they are saving money compared to open apis and can get much better quality inference!!

other inference providers that can secure compute are popping up bc most enterprises don’t actually need four nines—they have a backup provider that can eat inference if there’s downtime

also serving 72B and under models and making kernels for them is now not rocket science (used to be only a few shops like deepinfra could do it well)

there’s other ways to save on costs, like prompt compression (getting good), better tools like Context dev web highlights, and actually using the right model for your task (most don’t)

but getting your own compute or working with a neo-neo cloud is increasingly a good option

if anyone needs advice on reducing costs or needs GPUs happy to advise over dm!

please only dm if you spend over 50k/mo on inference. under that just negotiate cheaper inference rates with neo-neoclouds (they may not advertise that they negotiate, but they def do)
